summary: Rotate the array right by k steps in place.
mainInsight: Reduce k modulo n. Reversing the whole array, then the first k elements, then the remaining n - k elements yields the rotation in O(n) time and O(1) space. A cyclic-replacement variant moves each element to (i + k) % n following cycles.

approaches.name: Extra array
approaches.summary: result[(i + k) % n] = nums[i], copy back.

approaches.name: Three reversals
approaches.summary: Reverse all, then [0, k), then [k, n).

approaches.name: Cyclic replacement
approaches.summary: Move elements along cycles of the i -> (i + k) % n permutation.

commonMistakes: Using the extra array when O(1) space is required

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?

cards.answer: Reduce k modulo n, then reverse the whole array, the first k elements and the remaining ones. Clue: A right rotation by k moves the last k elements to the front, and k can exceed the length, so reduce k and rearrange in place with reversals.
keyPoints: A right rotation by k moves the last k elements to the front, and k can exceed the length, so reduce k and rearrange in place with reversals.
cards.explanation: Reversing everything and then each of the two parts puts the last k elements in front while keeping their inner order.

rubric.technique: Reduce k modulo n, then reverse the whole array, the first k elements and the remaining ones

promptVariants: Which sequence of operations rotates an array right by k in place?
How can reversals implement a rotation?
options: Reverse all, then the first k and the last n - k
Reverse only the first k elements of the array
Sort the array and shift every element by k places
Swap element i with element i + k for each index i
cards.answer: Reverse all, then the first k and the last n - k
cards.explanation: Reversing all moves the last k to the front reversed; reversing each part restores their order.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Swap element i with element i + k for ea: That is not a rotation and overflows the array.

promptVariants: Why must k be reduced modulo n, and what happens if it is not?
What does k >= n mean for a rotation?
cards.answer: Rotating by n returns the original array, so only k mod n matters. Without the reduction the slice indices or reversal ranges go out of bounds (and `k = 0 mod n` must be a no-op).

cards.explanation: Three reversals touch each element at most twice.

options: [1, 2]: rotating by more than n has no effect
cards.explanation: Three single-step rotations of two elements equal one.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[1, 2]: rotating by more than n has no e: Only multiples of n have no effect.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[2, 1] after three full swaps: Each step is one position, not a swap.
